<reason>Both sides agreed the decisive question is what happens when age verification fails, and CON won that comparison. CON's asymmetry argument—design law leaves the lying fourteen-year-old on a safe-default account, while a ban legally declares her an adult and hands her the full engagement product with open DMs—survived PRO's strongest pressure. PRO's Q1 (contact harms) was answered by pointing to "private-by-default" already in the opening, and CON flipped it by noting PRO's own scoping exempts the messaging apps where sextortion lives. CON's "pick one" attack—platforms can't be unregulable on visible design surfaces yet reliably regulable on invisible birthdays via the same fines—was never squarely met; PRO's "one number vs. many rules" reply ignored the visibility point. PRO did land a real hit with Q2 (CON's alternative also needs verification, weakening the "identity infrastructure" objection), and PRO's "exception, not architecture" framing plus the cohort-norm argument kept the debate competitive. But PRO's "invisible failure" claim depended on contact harms CON had already covered, and PRO's convergence toward "ban the machine's access to the child" partly conceded CON's ground. Both sides had a clipped turn, roughly cancelling.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Turn 8 A1: CON answered PRO's contact-harm pressure by invoking private-by-default contact rules from its opening, then inverted the charge—under the ban the lying child is legally thirty and fully discoverable, and PRO's own carve-out keeps messaging (the sextortion vector) open. This neutralized PRO's central "invisible failure" line.</best_rebuttal>
